questions.q: Why should a migration inventory be pulled from system catalogs like sys.objects rather than from existing documentation?
options: Documentation is usually stale, and undocumented objects are exactly the ones that break a migration late
System catalogs are faster to query than reading a document
Documentation never contains object names
System catalogs automatically convert objects to the target platform
questions.explain: Relying on documentation risks missing undocumented objects, which tend to cause the most damage when discovered late in a migration.

questions.q: Why are cross-database queries and linked server calls flagged as high-risk dependencies in this lesson?
options: They are trivial in SQL Server but often have no equivalent form on the target platform
They never appear in real SQL Server databases
They are automatically migrated by every target platform's native tools
They only affect read-only reporting queries
questions.explain: SQL Server's four-part names, OPENQUERY, and linked servers don't translate directly to Oracle database links, PostgreSQL foreign data wrappers, or MySQL federated tables.

questions.q: Why is application-embedded SQL described as often the hardest dependency category to find during assessment?
options: It lives in application code, not the database, so a database-only inventory never surfaces it
It is always clearly documented in the application's README
It never actually affects a migration's timeline
It only exists in applications written before 2010
questions.explain: Hardcoded T-SQL, ORM-generated SQL Server syntax, and reporting tools pointed at tables directly all live outside the database and are easy to undercount.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when should a team identify features with no target-platform equivalent?
options: Early, during assessment — before committing to a timeline, not after development has started
It doesn't matter, since every SQL Server feature has a direct equivalent on every platform
Only after the migration has gone live
During the final testing and cutover phase only
questions.explain: Finding a parity gap during assessment is a planning problem; finding it mid-development turns it into a costly, disruptive one.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend estimating schema conversion, code conversion, data movement, application changes, and testing/cutover separately rather than extrapolating from one number?
options: Each category has a different multiplier once real dependencies surface, and extrapolating from one category is usually wrong by two or three times
Separate estimates are required by law for database migrations
It makes the total estimate smaller and easier to approve
Only schema conversion actually takes meaningful time
questions.explain: Teams that estimate only schema conversion and extrapolate a total are almost always significantly wrong, per this lesson.
